approachQuestion.prompt:
A community room can host only one workshop at a time. Each workshop has a start time and a finish time, with start < finish. Two workshops are compatible when one finishes at or before the other starts. Given an unsorted list of workshops, return the largest possible number that can be hosted.

Example 1: [(1,4), (3,5), (0,6), (5,7), (8,9)] → 3, by choosing (1,4), (5,7), and (8,9).
Example 2: [(2,3), (3,5), (1,3)] → 2; finishing and starting at time 3 is allowed.
Example 3: [(0,10)] → 1.
constraints: The input is an unsorted list of n workshops; 0 ≤ n ≤ 100,000.
Each start and finish is an integer with 0 ≤ start < finish ≤ 1,000,000,000.
Return only the maximum count. Do not modify the input. All comparisons and arithmetic take O(1), with no overflow.

options.text: Copy the workshops, order them by increasing finish time, then scan in that order. Accept a workshop whenever its start is at or after the finish of the last accepted one.
options.feedback: Among remaining workshops, the one that finishes first leaves at least as much time for every later choice. Repeating that safe choice yields a maximum-size compatible set.

options.text: Copy the workshops, order them by increasing start time, and accept each one that does not overlap the last accepted workshop.
options.feedback: Starting first can occupy the room too long. On [(0,10), (1,2), (2,3)], this picks (0,10) and returns 1, while the last two workshops give 2.

options.text: Repeatedly choose the available workshop with the shortest duration, remove every workshop that conflicts with it, and continue.
options.feedback: A short workshop can conflict with two compatible workshops. On [(0,100), (99,102), (101,201)], choosing (99,102) prevents choosing both (0,100) and (101,201), so the result can be smaller than the optimum.

options.text: Try every subset of workshops, keep the largest subset whose members are pairwise compatible, and return its size.
options.feedback: This method can find the right answer, but it enumerates subsets instead of using the ordering and compatibility structure to make a direct sequence of choices.

feedback.reason: Check whether each local rule preserves the possibility of a largest compatible schedule, then distinguish a proof-backed rule from an unsupported shortcut.
details: Copy the workshops and order them by increasing finish time. Scan once, accepting a workshop if it starts at or after the finish time of the last accepted workshop. If finish times tie, any deterministic order is valid; tied workshops cannot both add room time beyond the same boundary.

An earliest-finishing accepted workshop can replace the first workshop of an optimal schedule without reducing room for later workshops. Accept touching endpoints under the stated rule. This maximizes count, not arbitrary workshop value.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze the fixed `sort-by-finish-and-accept` method. It copies the input and sorts the copy using stable top-down merge sort with one reusable merge buffer, then scans once. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Do not count the input or returned count as auxiliary space.
constraints: The sort is comparison-based stable merge sort; each comparison and assignment takes O(1).
The copy and merge buffer are auxiliary storage. The input and returned scalar are excluded.

options.text: Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n)
Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(1)
Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n log n)

feedback.reason: Sorting dominates one constant-state finish-time scan.
details: Sorting dominates the scan and takes O(n log n) time. The copied records and reusable merge buffer together take O(n) auxiliary space; the scan itself needs only constant state. The output is a scalar and is excluded.
Worst-case comparison sort is stable top-down merge sort on an input copy with a reusable linear merge buffer; input and output are excluded.
